This notebook contains the analysis behind the MD BGE (Baltimore Gas and Electric)
rate report. Starting from CAIRO simulation outputs on S3, it computes every statistic that
appears in the report narrative (`index.qmd`).

The functions doing the actual data crunching live in
[`lib/rates_analysis/rate_case_funcs.py`](../../../lib/rates_analysis/rate_case_funcs.py), a
module generalized over state, batch, and scenario so it can be reused for other utilities
and future tariff designs (e.g. a flat-rate heat pump tariff) without changes. This notebook
just calls those functions with MD BGE's specific state/batch/scenario values.

The analysis follows the report's arc:

1. **Bill-increase incidence today** — how often switching from natural gas to a heat pump
   raises a customer's total energy bill under MD BGE's current default rates.
2. **Cross-subsidization** — the Bill Alignment Test (BAT), showing heat pump customers
   systematically overpay for electric delivery under today's rates.
3. **A tech-specific seasonal rate** — the one reform tariff CAIRO has calibrated so far,
   and what it does to the cross-subsidy, to bill incidence, and to a representative
   household's monthly bills.
4. **What's blocked** — a time-of-use rate and a flat-rate tech-specific design are both
   discussed in the report, but neither has a CAIRO scenario yet; this notebook flags those
   gaps explicitly rather than fabricating numbers for them.

## Parameters

Batch and tariff-fetch pin (`RDP_REF`) live in `batch_config.yaml` alongside this report, not
hardcoded here, so re-running against a new batch is a one-file change. `RDP_REF` is a fixed
git commit SHA (not `main`) — the exact `rate-design-platform` commit that introduced the
scenario/tariff configs this batch was run against — so tariff JSONs are always fetched from
the code that actually produced this batch's numbers, even if `main` moves on later.

```{python}
#| label: params

_batch_config = yaml.safe_load(Path("../batch_config.yaml").read_text())

STATE = _batch_config["STATE"]
BATCH = _batch_config["BATCH"]
RDP_REF = _batch_config["RDP_REF"]
UTILITY = "bge"
YEAR = 2025

RESIDUAL = "percustomer"  # percustomer or epmc

BILL_COL = "energy_total_bill" # "energy_total_bill" (baseline), "energy_total_bill_lmi_48", or "energy_total_bill_lmi_100"

DEFAULT_SCENARIO = _batch_config["BASELINE_BILL_SCENARIO"]
SEASONAL_SCENARIO = f"hp_seasonal_{RESIDUAL}_passthrough"
FLAT_SCENARIO = f"hp_flat_{RESIDUAL}_passthrough"

print(f"state={STATE}  batch={BATCH}  rdp_ref={RDP_REF}  utility={UTILITY}  bill_col={BILL_COL}")
```

Batch `md_20260803_a` has two calibrated scenarios for MD BGE, each run at two stages:

- `precalc` — ResStock upgrade 00 (today's mixed heating population), tariff as filed/priced.
- `calibrated` — ResStock upgrade 02 (same buildings retrofitted to heat pumps), tariff
  recalibrated to meet each subclass's revenue requirement under that scenario's design.

| Scenario | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `default` | MD BGE's current default residential tariff (a single rate schedule for all residential customers). |
| `hp_seasonal_percustomer_passthrough` | A subclass-differentiated pair of tariffs, assigned automatically by each building's modeled heating type (`has_hp`), not by customer choice: the heat-pump subclass gets a seasonal volumetric delivery rate (same fixed charge as `default`); the non-heat-pump subclass gets its own separate, recalibrated tariff (`non-hp_base_percustomer_passthrough`) rather than staying on `default`, since the revenue no longer collected from the heat-pump subclass has to be made up somewhere. The residual (non-marginal-cost) revenue requirement is allocated per customer within each subclass. |

No time-of-use or flat-rate heat-pump scenario exists yet in MD BGE's pipeline
config — the report bullets that depend on those are flagged as blocked below, not filled in
with invented numbers.

Every bill-change comparison in this notebook (every `bill_delta_between_segments()` and
`plot_bill_change_quadrants()` call) reads the `BILL_COL` column set in the params cell
above — currently **`{python} BILL_COL`**. Leaving it at `energy_total_bill` compares
baseline (undiscounted) bills; switching it to `energy_total_bill_lmi_48` or
`energy_total_bill_lmi_100` reruns every comparison below net of Maryland's OHEP low-income
bill discount, at 48% or 100% participation respectively.

## Import data

The master bills and BAT tables are pre-built, Hive-partitioned parquet datasets — one row
per building per month (bills) or per building (BAT) — with ResStock metadata columns
already joined in. We load all four segments as LazyFrames; nothing is materialized until a
later cell filters and collects what it needs.

```{python}
#| label: ingest

SEG_DEFAULT_PRECALC = segment_name(DEFAULT_SCENARIO, "precalc")
SEG_DEFAULT_CALIBRATED = segment_name(DEFAULT_SCENARIO, "calibrated")
SEG_SEASONAL_PRECALC = segment_name(SEASONAL_SCENARIO, "precalc")
SEG_SEASONAL_CALIBRATED = segment_name(SEASONAL_SCENARIO, "calibrated")
SEG_FLAT_PRECALC = segment_name(FLAT_SCENARIO, "precalc")
SEG_FLAT_CALIBRATED = segment_name(FLAT_SCENARIO, "calibrated")

bills_default_precalc = load_master_bills(STATE, BATCH, SEG_DEFAULT_PRECALC)
bills_default_calibrated = load_master_bills(STATE, BATCH, SEG_DEFAULT_CALIBRATED)
bills_seasonal_precalc = load_master_bills(STATE, BATCH, SEG_SEASONAL_PRECALC)
bills_seasonal_calibrated = load_master_bills(STATE, BATCH, SEG_SEASONAL_CALIBRATED)
```

Let's look at a sample of the `default_precalc` bills to see what's in the table, and check
the sample size — how many ResStock buildings we have, and how many actual MD BGE
residential customers they represent once we sum ResStock's sample weights.

```{python}
#| label: sample-size

_sample = cast(
    pl.DataFrame,
    bills_default_precalc
    .filter(pl.col("month") == "Annual")
    .select("bldg_id", "weight", "postprocess_group.heating_type_v2", "postprocess_group.has_hp", "energy_total_bill")
    .collect(),
)
print(_sample.head())

n_resstock_bldgs = _sample["bldg_id"].n_unique()
n_utility_customers = float(_sample["weight"].sum())
report_vars["n_resstock_bldgs"] = n_resstock_bldgs
report_vars["n_utility_customers"] = n_utility_customers
print(f"Unique ResStock buildings: {n_resstock_bldgs:,}")
print(f"Total MD BGE residential customers (sum of weights): {n_utility_customers:,.0f}")
```

Every building appears in all four segments (`default`/`hp_seasonal_percustomer_passthrough`
× `precalc`/`calibrated`) — confirmed by checking that each segment's `bldg_id` set is
identical, which is what makes the same-tariff before/after comparisons and same-stage
cross-scenario comparisons below valid (they're diffing the same population against itself).

## Bill-increase incidence switching from natural gas to a heat pump, under today's rate

How often does a natural-gas-heated MD BGE home end up with a *higher* total annual
energy bill (electric + gas) after switching to a heat pump, if nothing about the rate design
changes? We diff each building's annual **`{python} BILL_COL`** between `default_precalc`
(today's HVAC, today's tariff) and `default_calibrated` (same building retrofitted to a heat
pump, same tariff family, recalibrated for the new load) — a same-scenario,
before/after-retrofit comparison — restricted to buildings whose baseline heating fuel is
natural gas.

```{python}
#| label: compute-natgas-hp-delta-default

delta_natgas_default = bill_delta_between_segments(
    STATE, BATCH, SEG_DEFAULT_PRECALC, SEG_DEFAULT_CALIBRATED, bill_col=BILL_COL
).filter(pl.col("heating_type_v2") == "natgas")

incidence_natgas_default = bill_change_incidence(delta_natgas_default)
incidence_natgas_default
```

```{python}
#| label: report-vars-natgas-hp-delta-default

report_vars["pct_natgas_hp_bill_increase_default"] = incidence_natgas_default["pct_increase"]
report_vars["pct_natgas_hp_bill_decrease_default"] = incidence_natgas_default["pct_decrease"]
report_vars["mean_natgas_hp_bill_increase_default"] = incidence_natgas_default["mean_delta"]
report_vars["median_natgas_hp_bill_increase_default"] = incidence_natgas_default["median_delta"]
```

**`{python} f"{report_vars['pct_natgas_hp_bill_increase_default']:.0%}"` of natural-gas-heated
MD BGE homes would see their total annual energy bill go up** after switching to a heat
pump under today's rate — a mean increase of `{python} f"${report_vars['mean_natgas_hp_bill_increase_default']:,.0f}"`
a year (median `{python} f"${report_vars['median_natgas_hp_bill_increase_default']:,.0f}"`).
The rest see a decrease, mostly from avoided gas costs outweighing the added electric load.

## Heat pump customers are overpaying for delivery today

Even setting bill *changes* aside, existing heat pump customers already pay more for
electric delivery than their incremental cost of service justifies — the Bill Alignment Test
(BAT) quantifies this directly. BAT values are only meaningful at the `precalc` stage (see
the module docstring in `rate_case_funcs.py`): the `calibrated` stage's revenue requirement is
deliberately inflated for calibration purposes, so its BAT is not a valid cross-subsidy
measure even though the bills themselves are correct there.

```{python}
#| label: hp-bat-summary-default

bat_default_hp = hp_bat_summary(STATE, BATCH, DEFAULT_SCENARIO, bat_col=f"BAT_{RESIDUAL}_delivery")
bat_default_hp
```

```{python}
#| label: report-vars-hp-bat-default

report_vars["hp_overpay_mean_default"] = bat_default_hp["mean_per_year"]
report_vars["hp_overpay_total_millions_default"] = bat_default_hp["total_per_year_millions"]
report_vars["hp_share_of_households_default"] = bat_default_hp["n_weighted"] / n_utility_customers
```

**Heat pump customers on the default rate overpay for delivery by an average of
`{python} f"${report_vars['hp_overpay_mean_default']:,.0f}"` a year** — `{python} f"${report_vars['hp_overpay_total_millions_default']:.1f}"`
million a year in total across MD BGE's roughly `{python} f"{report_vars['hp_share_of_households_default']:.0%}"`
heat-pump-heated residential population. That overpayment isn't unique to heat pumps — it's
a feature of MD BGE's uniform volumetric delivery rate. The same table, split by
baseline heating type, shows every all-electric subclass overpaying and every fossil-fuel
subclass underpaying relative to their delivery cost of service:

```{python}
#| label: tbl-bat-by-heating-type
#| tbl-cap: "Average delivery revenue, cost of service, and over/underpayment by baseline heating type (MD BGE, default rate)."

_bat_by_type = (
    add_heating_label(
        bat_by_group(
            STATE,
            BATCH,
            DEFAULT_SCENARIO,
            bat_col=f"BAT_{RESIDUAL}_delivery",
            residual=RESIDUAL,
        ),
        code_col="postprocess_group.heating_type_v2",
    )
    .drop("postprocess_group.heating_type_v2")
    .with_columns(
        pl.col("heating_label").cast(pl.Enum(HEATING_ORDER)),
        (pl.col("revenue_per_customer") / pl.col("cost_of_service_per_customer")).alias(
            "revenue_over_cos"
        ),
    )
    .sort("heating_label")
    .select(
        "heating_label",
        "revenue_per_customer",
        "residual_per_customer",
        "marginal_cost_per_customer",
        "cost_of_service_per_customer",
        "revenue_over_cos",
        "mean_per_year",
        "n_weighted",
    )
)
_bat_by_type_gt = (
    GT(_bat_by_type, rowname_col="heating_label")
    .fmt_currency(
        columns=[
            "revenue_per_customer",
            "residual_per_customer",
            "marginal_cost_per_customer",
            "cost_of_service_per_customer",
            "mean_per_year",
        ],
        decimals=0,
    )
    .fmt_number(columns="revenue_over_cos", decimals=2)
    .fmt_number(columns="n_weighted", decimals=0)
    .cols_label(
        revenue_per_customer="Avg. revenue",
        residual_per_customer="Avg. residual cost",
        marginal_cost_per_customer="Avg. marginal cost",
        cost_of_service_per_customer="Avg. cost of service",
        revenue_over_cos="Avg. revenue / COS",
        mean_per_year="Avg. over/underpayment",
        n_weighted="Weighted customers",
    )
    .tab_stubhead(label="Baseline heating type")
    .tab_source_note(f"Positive over/underpayment = overpaying delivery cost of service; negative = underpaying. Per-customer figures are weight-averaged. Residual allocator = {RESIDUAL}.")
    .tab_options(**get_switchbox_gt_tab_options())
)
display_gt(_bat_by_type_gt)
```

CAIRO also exports each building's actual annual kWh consumption (`billing_kwh_annual.parquet`,
alongside the standard master bills/BAT tables but only in the raw per-run output, not yet
promoted to a master table), so we can show the full delivery revenue / cost of service /
cross-subsidy picture by subclass in dollar and kWh terms together, not just the average
over/underpayment above.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-cos-by-subclass
#| tbl-cap: "Delivery revenue, cost of service, and cross-subsidy by heating-type subclass (MD BGE, default rate)."

cos_tbl = cost_of_service_by_subclass(
    STATE, BATCH, UTILITY, DEFAULT_SCENARIO,
    bat_col=f"BAT_{RESIDUAL}_delivery",
    residual=RESIDUAL,
)

_cos_gt = (
    GT(cos_tbl, rowname_col="subclass")
    .cols_label(
        n_customers="Customers",
        pct_all_customers="% of customers",
        consumption_gwh="Consumption",
        pct_all_consumption="% of consumption",
        revenue_delivery="Delivery revenue",
        pct_all_revenue="% of revenue",
        marginal_cost="Marginal cost",
        residual="Residual",
        cost_of_service="Cost of service",
        pct_all_cost_of_service="% of cost",
        cross_subsidy="Cross-subsidy",
        pct_overpayment_vs_cos="Cross-subsidy ÷ COS",
    )
    .fmt_number(columns="n_customers", decimals=0, use_seps=True)
    .fmt_number(columns="consumption_gwh", decimals=1)
    .fmt_percent(columns=["pct_all_customers", "pct_all_consumption", "pct_all_revenue", "pct_all_cost_of_service"], decimals=1)
    .fmt_percent(columns="pct_overpayment_vs_cos", decimals=1)
    .fmt_currency(
        columns=["revenue_delivery", "marginal_cost", "residual", "cost_of_service", "cross_subsidy"],
        decimals=0,
    )
    .tab_stubhead(label="Baseline heating type")
    .tab_source_note(
        f"Cost of service = marginal cost + residual. "
        f"Positive cross-subsidy = overpaying delivery cost of service; negative = underpaying. "
        f"Residual allocator = {RESIDUAL}."
    )
    .tab_options(**get_switchbox_gt_tab_options())
)
display_gt(_cos_gt)
```

`cost_of_service` above is itself the sum of two differently-motivated pieces: the
**marginal cost** each subclass causes (`economic_burden_delivery`, the cost-causation-based
charge) and the **residual** (`residual_share_delivery`, the leftover revenue requirement —
fixed and sunk costs not attributable to any one customer — allocated across subclasses by
CAIRO's chosen allocator). Splitting them out shows *why* each subclass over- or underpays,
not just by how much.

```{python}
#| label: fig-revenue-requirement-breakdown
#| fig-cap: "MD BGE's residential delivery revenue requirement, split into marginal cost recovery and residual, by baseline heating-type subclass."

revreq_breakdown = revenue_requirement_breakdown_by_subclass(STATE, BATCH, UTILITY, DEFAULT_SCENARIO)
plot_revenue_requirement_breakdown(revreq_breakdown)
```

```{python}
#| label: report-vars-revenue-requirement-breakdown

_revreq_total = revreq_breakdown.filter(pl.col("subclass") == "All customers")
report_vars["revreq_marginal_cost_millions"] = (
    _revreq_total.filter(pl.col("component") == "Marginal cost")["value"][0] / 1e6
)
report_vars["revreq_residual_millions"] = (
    _revreq_total.filter(pl.col("component") == "Residual")["value"][0] / 1e6
)
report_vars["revreq_pct_residual"] = report_vars["revreq_residual_millions"] / (
    report_vars["revreq_marginal_cost_millions"] + report_vars["revreq_residual_millions"]
)
```

Across all of MD BGE's residential customers, `{python} f"${report_vars['revreq_marginal_cost_millions']:.1f}"`
million a year of the delivery revenue requirement recovers marginal cost, while
`{python} f"${report_vars['revreq_residual_millions']:.1f}"` million —
`{python} f"{report_vars['revreq_pct_residual']:.0%}"` of the total — is residual. That
imbalance holds within every subclass too (@fig-revenue-requirement-breakdown): residual
revenue is several times larger than marginal cost for every baseline heating type, which is
exactly why the residual *allocator* — not the marginal-cost charge — is what mostly
determines whether a subclass over- or underpays in the table above.

## When are delivery costs actually incurred?

MD BGE's delivery marginal costs — bulk transmission and distribution +
sub-transmission capacity — are hourly series covering all 8,760 hours of 2025.
Both are zero most of the year and spike only in a small number of hours, which
is exactly the timing mismatch a uniform volumetric rate can't reflect.

```{python}
#| label: load-mc-heatmap-data

mc_heatmap_df = load_delivery_mc_heatmap(STATE, UTILITY, YEAR)
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-mc-heatmap-bulk-tx
#| fig-cap: "Hourly marginal bulk transmission capacity costs, MD BGE, 2025."

plot_mc_heatmap(
    mc_heatmap_df, "mc_bulk_tx",
    title="Bulk Transmission — Marginal Capacity Cost by Hour",
    high_color=SB_COLORS["midnight"],
)
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-mc-heatmap-dist-sub-tx
#| fig-cap: "Hourly marginal distribution and sub-transmission capacity costs, MD BGE, 2025."

plot_mc_heatmap(
    mc_heatmap_df, "mc_dist_sub_tx",
    title="Distribution + Sub-Transmission — Marginal Capacity Cost by Hour",
    high_color=SB_COLORS["carrot"],
)
```

## A time-of-use rate doesn't fix it — but we can't show that yet

::: {.callout-note}
No time-of-use scenario has been run for this batch — `pipeline_bge.yaml` only
defines `default` and `hp_seasonal_percustomer_passthrough` scenarios so far. Once a TOU
scenario exists, the exact same `hp_bat_summary()` call used above answers this — no new
code needed.
:::

## Fixing the cross-subsidy with a tech-specific seasonal rate

The report describes two ways to eliminate the heat-pump delivery cross-subsidy: raise the
fixed charge (lowering the volumetric rate for everyone, revenue-neutral), or lower the
volumetric rate specifically for heat pump customers via a tech-specific rate. The one reform
tariff CAIRO has calibrated so far — `hp_seasonal_percustomer_passthrough` — takes the second
path: a seasonal volumetric delivery rate for the heat-pump subclass, paired with a separate
recalibrated tariff for the non-heat-pump subclass, with the residual revenue requirement
allocated per customer within each subclass.

### What the tariff actually changed

We read both tariffs' calibrated URDB JSON directly to see what changed.

```{python}
#| label: load-tariffs

tariff_default = load_tariff_json(STATE, UTILITY, f"{UTILITY}_default_calibrated", RDP_REF)
tariff_seasonal = load_tariff_json(STATE, UTILITY, f"{UTILITY}_{SEASONAL_SCENARIO}_calibrated", RDP_REF)
tariff_flat = load_tariff_json(STATE, UTILITY, f"{UTILITY}_{FLAT_SCENARIO}_calibrated", RDP_REF)
rates_default = extract_tariff_rates(tariff_default)
rates_seasonal = extract_tariff_rates(tariff_seasonal)
rates_flat = extract_tariff_rates(tariff_flat)
print("default:", rates_default)
print("seasonal:", rates_seasonal)
print("flat:", rates_flat)
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-tariff-months
#| tbl-cap: "Volumetric delivery rate by month: today's default rate vs. the seasonal and flat heat-pump rates."

_tariff_months = tariff_month_rate_table(
    {
        "Default rate (¢/kWh)": rates_default,
        "Seasonal HP rate (¢/kWh)": rates_seasonal,
        "Flat HP rate (¢/kWh)": rates_flat,
    }
)

_tariff_months_gt = (
    GT(_tariff_months, rowname_col="month")
    .fmt_number(
        columns=[
            "Default rate (¢/kWh)",
            "Seasonal HP rate (¢/kWh)",
            "Flat HP rate (¢/kWh)",
        ],
        decimals=2,
    )
    .tab_stubhead(label="Month")
    .tab_options(**get_switchbox_gt_tab_options())
)
display_gt(_tariff_months_gt)
```

```{python}
#| label: report-vars-tariff-rates

report_vars["tariff_default_fixed_charge"] = rates_default["fixed_charge"]
report_vars["tariff_seasonal_fixed_charge"] = rates_seasonal["fixed_charge"]
report_vars["tariff_seasonal_summer_cents"] = rates_seasonal["period_rates"][0] * 100
report_vars["tariff_seasonal_winter_cents"] = rates_seasonal["period_rates"][1] * 100
report_vars["tariff_default_avg_cents"] = (
    sum(rates_default["period_rates"][rates_default["month_to_period"][m]] for m in MONTH_ORDER)
    / len(MONTH_ORDER)
    * 100
)
```

::: {.callout-important}
**The calibrated seasonal tariff keeps exactly the same $`{python} f"{report_vars['tariff_default_fixed_charge']:.0f}"`/month
fixed charge as the default rate** — we confirmed this both in the tariff JSON and in the
master bills' `elec_fixed_charge` column (identical for every building in both scenarios).
CAIRO's "per-customer" residual allocation here is expressed entirely through the seasonal
*volumetric* rate, not a higher fixed charge.

What this scenario answers is: a tech-specific rate that lowers the volumetric rate for heat
pump customers, done seasonally. The summer rate
(`{python} f"{report_vars['tariff_seasonal_summer_cents']:.2f}"`¢/kWh, Jun–Sep) is close to
today's `{python} f"{report_vars['tariff_default_avg_cents']:.2f}"`¢/kWh average, while the
winter rate drops to `{python} f"{report_vars['tariff_seasonal_winter_cents']:.2f}"`¢/kWh
(Jan–May, Oct–Dec) — confirming the report's framing that a seasonal tech-specific design
would hold the summer rate roughly flat while cutting the winter rate.
:::

### Does the seasonal rate actually eliminate the cross-subsidy?

`hp_bat_summary()` on the `default` scenario already gave us the "before" number above
(`{python} f"${report_vars['hp_overpay_mean_default']:,.0f}"`/yr). `compare_bat_across_scenarios()`
adds the "after" number in the same table, so we can see both without a second, redundant
call:

```{python}
#| label: tbl-bat-before-after
#| tbl-cap: "Heat pump customers' average delivery overpayment, before and after the seasonal reform tariff."

_bat_compare = compare_bat_across_scenarios(
    STATE, BATCH, [DEFAULT_SCENARIO, SEASONAL_SCENARIO], bat_col=f"BAT_{RESIDUAL}_delivery"
)
_bat_compare_gt = (
    GT(_bat_compare.select("scenario", "mean_per_year", "total_per_year_millions"), rowname_col="scenario")
    .fmt_currency(columns="mean_per_year", decimals=0)
    .fmt_currency(columns="total_per_year_millions", decimals=1)
    .cols_label(mean_per_year="Average overpayment ($/yr)", total_per_year_millions="Total ($M/yr)")
    .tab_stubhead(label="Scenario")
    .tab_options(**get_switchbox_gt_tab_options())
)
display_gt(_bat_compare_gt)
```

```{python}
#| label: report-vars-bat-seasonal

report_vars["hp_overpay_mean_seasonal"] = float(
    _bat_compare.filter(pl.col("scenario") == SEASONAL_SCENARIO)["mean_per_year"][0]
)
```

Under the seasonal rate, the heat-pump subclass's average delivery overpayment falls to
essentially zero (`{python} f"${report_vars['hp_overpay_mean_seasonal']:,.2f}"`/yr) — CAIRO
calibrated the seasonal volumetric rate specifically to close this gap, so this confirms the
calibration worked rather than solving anything new.

### Isolating the rate-design effect, before anyone retrofits

This comparison holds HVAC equipment fixed and changes only the tariff, so the bill change it
measures is purely a rate-design effect, not a retrofit effect. To be precise about what's
being compared:

- **Population**: every MD BGE residential customer, split into the two subclasses
  used by the reform tariff — the **heat-pump subclass** (buildings our model assigns a heat
  pump to, `has_hp == true`) and the **non-heat-pump subclass** (everyone else). This split
  is automatic, based on each building's modeled heating type — not a choice a customer makes.
- **HVAC, before and after**: base/pre-retrofit (`upgrade=00`) for both subclasses in both the
  "before" and "after" case. Nobody has actually installed a heat pump in either segment being
  compared here — `default_precalc` and `hp_seasonal_percustomer_passthrough_precalc` are both
  `upgrade=00` runs.
- **Tariff, before**: today's default rate, applied identically to both subclasses.
- **Tariff, after**: the reform tariff pair — the heat-pump subclass moves to the seasonal
  rate examined above, and the non-heat-pump subclass moves to its own separate, recalibrated
  tariff (`non-hp_base_percustomer_passthrough`), not an unchanged default rate, since the
  revenue no longer collected from the heat-pump subclass has to be recovered somewhere.

```{python}
#| label: compute-ratedesign-delta

delta_ratedesign = bill_delta_between_segments(STATE, BATCH, SEG_DEFAULT_PRECALC, SEG_FLAT_PRECALC, bill_col=BILL_COL)

incidence_hp_ratedesign = bill_change_incidence(delta_ratedesign.filter(pl.col("has_hp")))
incidence_nonhp_ratedesign = bill_change_incidence(delta_ratedesign.filter(~pl.col("has_hp")))
print("heat-pump subclass, default -> seasonal rate:", incidence_hp_ratedesign)
print("non-heat-pump subclass, default -> recalibrated non-HP tariff:", incidence_nonhp_ratedesign)
```

```{python}
#| label: report-vars-ratedesign-delta

report_vars["hp_mean_bill_change_seasonal_ratedesign"] = incidence_hp_ratedesign["mean_delta"]
report_vars["pct_hp_bill_decrease_seasonal_ratedesign"] = incidence_hp_ratedesign["pct_decrease"]
report_vars["nonhp_mean_bill_change_seasonal_ratedesign"] = incidence_nonhp_ratedesign["mean_delta"]
report_vars["pct_nonhp_bill_increase_seasonal_ratedesign"] = incidence_nonhp_ratedesign["pct_increase"]
```

Every building in the heat-pump subclass sees its bill fall under the reform tariff — a mean
decrease of `{python} f"${-report_vars['hp_mean_bill_change_seasonal_ratedesign']:,.0f}"` a
year, even before any of them have installed a heat pump — because the seasonal rate was
calibrated to charge that subclass its (pre-retrofit) cost of service. That decrease has to
come from somewhere: the non-heat-pump subclass's recalibrated tariff raises their bills by a
mean of `{python} f"${report_vars['nonhp_mean_bill_change_seasonal_ratedesign']:,.0f}"` a
year, because removing the heat-pump subsidy shifts MD BGE's residual revenue
requirement onto everyone else.

The mean hides how that increase is distributed across the non-heat-pump subclass — most see
a small bump, but the distribution has a tail (@fig-hist-nonhp-ratedesign).

```{python}
#| label: fig-hist-nonhp-ratedesign
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of the annual bill change for the non-heat-pump subclass, from the default rate to the recalibrated non-HP tariff under the seasonal fair scenario (same, pre-retrofit HVAC throughout)."

plot_ratedesign_monthly_hist(
    delta_ratedesign.filter(~pl.col("has_hp")),
    incidence_nonhp_ratedesign["median_delta"],
)
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-cdf-nonhp-ratedesign2
#| fig-cap: "Cumulative share of non-heat-pump households by monthly bill change under the reform tariff, all non-HP vs. excluding electric resistance and heat-pump baseline heating types."

plot_ratedesign_cdf(
    delta_ratedesign.filter(~pl.col("has_hp")),
    incidence_nonhp_ratedesign["median_delta"],
)
```

### Does the seasonal rate change how many heat pump conversions save money?

We repeat the natural-gas → heat-pump retrofit comparison from the first section, but this
time under the seasonal reform tariff instead of the default rate.

```{python}
#| label: compute-natgas-hp-delta-seasonal

delta_natgas_seasonal = bill_delta_between_segments(
    STATE, BATCH, SEG_SEASONAL_PRECALC, SEG_SEASONAL_CALIBRATED, bill_col=BILL_COL
).filter(pl.col("heating_type_v2") == "natgas")

incidence_natgas_seasonal = bill_change_incidence(delta_natgas_seasonal)
incidence_natgas_seasonal
```

```{python}
#| label: report-vars-natgas-hp-delta-seasonal

report_vars["pct_natgas_hp_bill_increase_seasonal"] = incidence_natgas_seasonal["pct_increase"]
report_vars["pct_natgas_hp_bill_decrease_seasonal"] = incidence_natgas_seasonal["pct_decrease"]
report_vars["pct_pt_improvement_natgas_hp_savings"] = (
    (incidence_natgas_seasonal["pct_decrease"] - incidence_natgas_default["pct_decrease"]) * 100
)
```

Under the seasonal rate, only `{python} f"{report_vars['pct_natgas_hp_bill_increase_seasonal']:.0%}"`
of natural-gas homes would see a bill increase after switching to a heat pump — down from
`{python} f"{report_vars['pct_natgas_hp_bill_increase_default']:.0%}"` under the default rate.
That's `{python} f"{report_vars['pct_pt_improvement_natgas_hp_savings']:.0f}"` more percentage
points of natural-gas customers who'd come out ahead switching to a heat pump.

### A representative household's monthly bills, before and after

To make the seasonal design concrete, we pick the weighted-median natural-gas-heated MD
BGE home (by annual `energy_total_bill` today) and follow that same building through
to a heat pump, under the seasonal rate — showing its actual monthly electric bill, split
into delivery and supply.

```{python}
#| label: pick-representative-household

_natgas_baseline = cast(
    pl.DataFrame,
    bills_default_precalc
    .filter(pl.col("month") == "Annual")
    .filter(pl.col("postprocess_group.heating_type_v2") == "natgas")
    .select("bldg_id", "weight", "energy_total_bill")
    .collect(),
)
median_natgas_bldg_id = weighted_median_bldg_id(_natgas_baseline, "energy_total_bill")
print(f"Representative natural-gas-heated building: bldg_id={median_natgas_bldg_id}")
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-monthly-bill-representative
#| fig-cap: "A representative MD BGE home's monthly electric bill after switching to a heat pump, under the seasonal rate."

plot_monthly_bill_components(
    monthly_bill_components(STATE, BATCH, SEG_SEASONAL_CALIBRATED, median_natgas_bldg_id),
    title="Monthly electric bill after switching to a heat pump (seasonal rate)",
)
```
```{python}
#| label: fig-monthly-bill-representative-default
#| fig-cap: "A representative MD BGE home's monthly electric bill after switching to a heat pump, under the seasonal rate."

plot_monthly_bill_components(
    monthly_bill_components(STATE, BATCH, SEG_DEFAULT_CALIBRATED, median_natgas_bldg_id),
    title="Monthly electric bill after switching to a heat pump (default rate)",
)
```
```{python}
#| label: report-vars-representative-household

_before_bill = float(
    _natgas_baseline.filter(pl.col("bldg_id") == median_natgas_bldg_id)["energy_total_bill"][0]
)
_after_bill = float(
    cast(
        pl.DataFrame,
        bills_seasonal_calibrated
        .filter((pl.col("bldg_id") == median_natgas_bldg_id) & (pl.col("month") == "Annual"))
        .select("energy_total_bill")
        .collect(),
    )["energy_total_bill"][0]
)
report_vars["representative_bldg_id"] = median_natgas_bldg_id
```

For this household, the annual energy bill goes from `{python} f"${report_vars['representative_annual_bill_before']:,.0f}"`
(natural gas + electric today) to `{python} f"${report_vars['representative_annual_bill_after']:,.0f}"`
(all-electric heat pump, seasonal rate) — and within that heat-pump bill, the delivery share
of each monthly bill is lowest in the winter months (Jan, Feb, Mar, Nov, Dec) precisely when
heating load — and total consumption — is highest, which is what the lower winter volumetric
rate is designed to do.

### The same household's annual bill, three ways

Putting the same building's annual bill side by side across all three states — natural gas
today, heat pump under today's default rate, and heat pump under the seasonal reform rate —
shows how much of the heat-pump bill increase the reform actually offsets.

```{python}
#| label: fig-bill-decomposed-representative
#| fig-cap: "Annual energy bill for the representative MD BGE natural-gas home: before heat pumps, after heat pumps at the default rate, and after heat pumps at the seasonal reform rate."

_before = annual_bill_components(STATE, BATCH, SEG_DEFAULT_PRECALC, median_natgas_bldg_id)
_after_default = annual_bill_components(STATE, BATCH, SEG_DEFAULT_CALIBRATED, median_natgas_bldg_id)
_after_seasonal = annual_bill_components(STATE, BATCH, SEG_SEASONAL_CALIBRATED, median_natgas_bldg_id)

fig_3bar_seasonal, seasonal_savings, seasonal_savings_pct, _, _ = plot_decomposed_bill_3bar(
    _before,
    _after_default,
    _after_seasonal,
    third_scenario_label="Heat pump\n(seasonal rate)",
    title="Seasonal rate narrows the heat pump bill increase",
)
report_vars["seasonal_reform_savings_dollar"] = seasonal_savings
report_vars["seasonal_reform_savings_pct"] = seasonal_savings_pct
report_vars["representative_annual_bill_after_default"] = sum(_after_default[k] for k in DECOMPOSED_BILL_COMPONENT_KEYS)
display_svg(fig_3bar_seasonal)
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-bill-decomposed-representative-flat
#| fig-cap: "Annual energy bill for the representative MD BGE natural-gas home: before heat pumps, after heat pumps at the default rate, and after heat pumps at the flat reform rate."

_after_flat = annual_bill_components(STATE, BATCH, SEG_FLAT_CALIBRATED, median_natgas_bldg_id)

fig_3bar_flat, flat_savings, flat_savings_pct, _, _ = plot_decomposed_bill_3bar(
    _before,
    _after_default,
    _after_flat,
    third_scenario_label="Heat pump\n(flat rate)",
    title="Flat rate narrows the heat pump bill increase",
)
report_vars["flat_reform_savings_dollar"] = flat_savings
report_vars["flat_reform_savings_pct"] = flat_savings_pct
report_vars["representative_annual_bill_after_flat"] = sum(_after_flat[k] for k in DECOMPOSED_BILL_COMPONENT_KEYS)
display_svg(fig_3bar_flat)
```

Even under the seasonal reform tariff, this household's heat-pump bill
(`{python} f"${report_vars['representative_annual_bill_after']:,.0f}"`) stays above its
original gas bill
(`{python} f"${report_vars['representative_annual_bill_before']:,.0f}"`) — the reform closes
part of the gap, cutting the default-rate heat-pump bill by
`{python} f"{report_vars['seasonal_reform_savings_pct']:.0%}"`
(`{python} f"${report_vars['seasonal_reform_savings_dollar']:,.0f}"`/yr), but doesn't erase the
increase entirely for this particular building.

The same decomposition under the **flat** reform tariff (@fig-bill-decomposed-representative-flat)
cuts the default-rate heat-pump bill by
`{python} f"{report_vars['flat_reform_savings_pct']:.0%}"`
(`{python} f"${report_vars['flat_reform_savings_dollar']:,.0f}"`/yr) for this household — a
`{python} f"{(report_vars['flat_reform_savings_pct'] - report_vars['seasonal_reform_savings_pct']) * 100:+.0f}"`-point
difference from the seasonal design.

### Where the incremental heat-pump bill comes from

The bill comparisons above show the *net* change in this household's annual bill. To see
*why* it changes, we decompose the same building's annual kWh, cost of service (marginal
cost + residual), and delivery bill (fixed + volumetric) into two portions: what it already
had as a natural-gas home ("existing"), and the extra load, marginal cost, and volumetric
bill that come from switching to a heat pump ("incremental"). The residual and the fixed
charge get no incremental split — both are flat, per-customer costs that, under
`{python} f"{RESIDUAL}"` residual allocation, don't move with one building's usage.

```{python}
#| label: fig-cost-breakdown-representative-default
#| fig-cap: "Annual kWh, cost of service, and delivery bill for the representative MD BGE natural-gas home, before and after switching to a heat pump, under the default rate."

cost_breakdown_default = representative_cost_data(
    STATE, UTILITY, BATCH, median_natgas_bldg_id, SEG_DEFAULT_CALIBRATED, residual=RESIDUAL,
)
plot_representative_cost_breakdown(
    cost_breakdown_default,
    title="Switching to a heat pump raises usage, marginal cost, and delivery bill — under the default rate",
)
```

Under the seasonal reform rate, the same household's incremental usage is priced
differently — the seasonal design charges winter (heating-season) kWh at a different rate
than the default tariff does — so the same incremental load translates into a different
split between marginal cost and delivery bill.

```{python}
#| label: fig-cost-breakdown-representative-seasonal
#| fig-cap: "Annual kWh, cost of service, and delivery bill for the representative MD BGE natural-gas home, before and after switching to a heat pump, under the seasonal reform rate."

cost_breakdown_seasonal = representative_cost_data(
    STATE,
    UTILITY,
    BATCH,
    median_natgas_bldg_id,
    SEG_SEASONAL_CALIBRATED,
    residual=RESIDUAL,
)
plot_representative_cost_breakdown(
    cost_breakdown_seasonal,
    title="Switching to a heat pump raises usage, marginal cost, and delivery bill — under the default rate",
)
```
